name: spy
intent: Record how a collaborator was actually called while the real system under test runs, so the test can assert on those interactions after the fact instead of predicting them up front.
problem: The behaviour under test depends on what the system under test does to its collaborators - which methods it calls, with which arguments, in which order - but return values do not reveal that traffic, and writing the expectations before the run either over-specifies the interaction or keeps the collaborator's real behaviour out of the test.
context: Unit and integration tests where the collaborator can be replaced or wrapped at a seam (constructor/DI, module substitution, virtual or interface method), where the recorded interaction is the assertion target, and where the team prefers arrange-act-assert (run real code, then inspect what was called) over a record/replay expectation DSL.
benefits: The test asserts only the interactions the requirement names, after the code has run, so calls nobody asserts on do not have to be predicted in advance.
A partial spy delegates to the real implementation by default, so the SUT is exercised end-to-end before the interaction is checked.
No expectation language to learn: the double is an ordinary object plus a call log, and assertions use the test framework's own matchers.
The recorded log is evidence: failures show exactly which calls happened with which arguments, which shortens debugging of unexpected interactions.
One recording double can serve many tests - recording is passive, so different tests can assert different subsets of the same traffic (unlike expectation-programmed mocks).
Pushes the suite toward state-first testing with interaction assertions only where the interaction really is the contract.
tradeoffs: Interaction coupling: asserting on recorded calls ties the test to the collaborator's call protocol, so refactors that preserve observable behaviour but change call shape break the suite.
Over-specification is easy and silent: exact arguments, counts, order and no-more-interactions assertions ossify incidental behaviour and produce brittle suites.
A spy that wraps the real collaborator still executes its side effects (mail, network, disk); the test must isolate them or the double must be partial by design.
Silent drift: a recording double keeps accepting calls when the real collaborator's signature or semantics change, unless the compiler or a contract test catches it.
Post-hoc assertions surface as delayed failures: the error appears at the assertion site, not at the interaction, which can obscure the intended contract for readers.
The call log is mutable shared state; concurrent executions race unless the log is synchronised or per-thread.
Framework reach is limited: final/static/private members and self-referencing code often cannot be spied, pushing tests toward looser seams or heavier agent-based tools.
Some ecosystems need code generation (Cuckoo, CMock) or bytecode instrumentation, adding build complexity for the double itself.

participants.responsibility: The production code that is exercised for real; it calls the spy through the collaborator's interface, unaware that it is being recorded.
Exposes the collaborator's interface, answers or delegates like the real collaborator, and appends every invocation (method, arguments, order, error) to a call log for later inspection.
The production object the spy wraps or replaces; when partial spying is used, its implementation produces the responses while the spy records the traffic.
Installs the spy at a seam, runs the SUT, then asserts against the recorded log (counts, arguments, relative order) during the assertion phase.
The constructor parameter, DI registration, module substitution or generated stub through which the spy is installed without editing the SUT.

use_cases: Verifying that a service actually sends the notification or publishes the event a requirement demands, after the business method ran.
Legacy code where only the collaborator can be replaced (no return-value seam): record calls to the repository, mailer or clock and assert what the code did with them.
Retry, batching and caching logic: assert call counts and argument sequences (for example three attempts with growing payloads) instead of poking internal counters.
Wrapping an existing object method (logger, HTTP client, even third-party code) to record usage without reimplementing its behaviour.
Pinning the interaction contract between two of your own components before extracting an interface or splitting a service.
Characterisation of legacy behaviour: record what the code calls today, then freeze the recording into the regression suite.

Java with Mockito: Mockito.spy(realObject) (or @Spy) creates a partial mock whose real methods run unless individually stubbed - Mockito's javadoc calls spy() the recommended way of creating partial mocks - and verify() then checks the recorded calls after the SUT ran.

JavaScript/TypeScript with Jest or Sinon.js: jest.spyOn(object, 'method') or sinon.spy(object, 'method') wraps an existing method so the original still executes while every call's arguments, return value, this value and thrown exception are recorded, then mockRestore()/sandbox.restore() puts the original back.

Python with the standard library: unittest.mock.patch(target, wraps=real) (or patch.object(..., wraps=real)) returns a Mock that forwards each call to the real object and records call_args_list/call_count - a partial spy without third-party tooling.
avoid_when: The assertion target is a return value or resulting state: a stub or fake is simpler and keeps the test free of interaction details.
The expected interaction sequence IS the behaviour under test (protocol handshake, ordered state machine): declare it with a mock/expectation DSL instead of asserting after the fact.
The collaborator cannot be substituted (final/static/private members, sealed types) and no honest seam exists: fix the design before reaching for instrumentation tools.
A working cheap implementation is enough (in-memory repository, deterministic clock): a fake is more reusable and less coupled to call shapes.
The only thing to assert is 'the method was called once': that is usually a proxy assertion for a missing state check.
anti_patterns: Assert-everything spies: recording and asserting every call (no-more-interactions checks, full argument decks) so the test restates the implementation and breaks on every refactor.
Spying as a substitute for design: wrapping a collaborator only because it is a hard-wired singleton or static call, instead of introducing a seam.
Partial spies with real side effects left in: letting the wrapped implementation send mail or hit the network, then calling it a unit test.
Mock/spy confusion: expecting the spy to fail on unexpected calls as a mock would; a recorded interaction is data, not enforcement.
Log assertions coupled to incidental arguments (timestamps, generated ids) that make the test nondeterministic.
design_principles: Separate verification styles: a spy asserts recorded interactions after the fact, a mock enforces expectations during the run; pick per test intent.
Least coupling: assert only the interactions the contract names; everything else stays free to evolve.
Dependency inversion and seam-first design: injecting the collaborator is what makes spying possible at all.
One recording double per collaborator role, reused across tests, keeps the suite's vocabulary consistent.
Observable behaviour first: prefer state or return-value assertions; use interaction assertions where the interaction is the contract.
best_practices: Install the spy at a seam (constructor, DI container, module substitution) and restore the original in teardown (restoreAllMocks, sandbox.restore, unstub) so tests stay isolated.
Keep one call log per test: create a fresh spy per test and never share mutable recording state.
Delegate to the real implementation by default and override only what the test needs, so the SUT still exercises genuine behaviour.
Assert the interactions the requirement names (recipient, payload, relative order), not incidental details such as timestamps or generated ids.
Pair the spy with state assertions for the primary outcome; the interaction log is secondary evidence.
When the tooling cannot reach the collaborator (final/static members), extract an interface instead of escalating to more invasive instrumentation.
sources: Meszaros, xUnit Test Patterns: Refactoring Test Code (2007) - Test Spy (Test Doubles part): a double that captures indirect outputs of the SUT for later verification. Catalogued as xunit-test-patterns.
